title: Risk-Free Rate
body:
The **risk-free rate** is the return obtainable with no risk of loss, in practice the yield on
a short-term government bond. It is the baseline every risky investment is measured against.

Its role in the [[Sharpe Ratio]] is to prevent a strategy from being credited with return
that required nothing. If bonds pay 4% and a fund returns 5% while swinging violently, the fund
produced 1% of return for all that risk, and subtracting the risk-free rate is what makes that
visible.

```
fund return        5%
risk-free rate     4%
excess return      1%       what the risk actually bought
```

The rate is not constant, so a Sharpe ratio computed over a long period uses a series rather
than one number, and the same strategy scores differently depending on the rate environment it
ran in. Comparing two funds from different decades without accounting for that produces a
meaningless comparison.

Risk-free is an idealisation. A government bond carries no default risk in the usual analysis
and still carries inflation risk, so the real return can be negative while the nominal return
is positive.
